Mentioning circularity and an infinite regress in the theologians' proof is unnecessary. They accept no separate immaterial being besides God. So it is enough, by their method, to show that a created thing cannot be a body or bodily. They need not also appeal to circularity or an infinite regress.

The objection does not refute the argument. The agent's priority over its effect is established, but the recipient need not come before what it receives; the reverse may be true. Form is a co-cause of matter and is prior to it in every way, as the author himself says elsewhere. Perhaps “recipient” here does not mean a recipient in the technical sense, but an external subject that bears an accident, in keeping with the rule that a subject must exist before its attribute. Yet that rule establishes only that the two—the subject and what is established in it—exist together. The stronger claim that the subject must come first needs separate proof. Comparing essence to a subject, and existence to its accidents, is also mistaken. In reality, essence is the reverse of existence; its unity and its added existence in the mind come from the intellect's analysis. The external reality of existence itself is not something the mind can reach and analyze in this way. — May God protect him.

The point is that essence is only a mental consideration. It does not create a real duality in a possible thing, nor a real capacity to receive or be received. A merely conceptual recipient need not exist before what it receives, even though a real recipient does. So how could a merely conceptual essence create a real duality in God, and thereby a real relation of making that would require the maker to precede what is made? The author is not saying that God's essence really makes His existence but does not precede it; God's essence is purely conceptual and disappears into existence, even in possible things—and all the more so in God.

This answers al-Tusi's reply in his commentary on Ibn Sina's Pointers, where he responds to al-Razi's objection about a recipient. Al-Tusi says that essence receives existence only when it exists in the mind, and cannot cause an external attribute while existing only in the mind. But once the intellect analyzes God as involving two aspects—essence and existence—it is also positing a distinction in reality. The intellect must then decide whether essence is the cause of existence, its recipient, or neither; and the same choices apply in reverse to existence.

If essence is the cause, it must exist before existence, because to posit a thing is to posit what necessarily follows from it. Even a possible essence, though only a mental consideration, is receptive when examined in itself, and existence is what it receives. So if one posits an essence for a possible thing, one must also posit it as receptive and prior in substance to what it receives. The same follows if one posits a necessary essence for God: it must be the cause of His existence and prior to it. All these problems arise from positing two aspects, even if only by the intellect.

If essence is receptive in the sense that a thing bears a quality—as four bears evenness—it would also have to be a cause, and the same problem follows. If it receives existence passively, it would be a possible essence, contradicting the claim that it is necessary. If it is neither cause nor recipient, there is nothing to unite essence and existence, leaving them separate as a stone lying beside a person. If existence is the cause or the recipient, the essence is not made real, since making real belongs to existence. If existence is a passive recipient, then essence becomes a changing quality added to existence. If it is neither cause nor recipient, the same separation follows. Most of these options also contradict the claim that what is necessary is existence and that essence is outside it.

There is another argument, beyond the one given in the notes on the First Journey. Essence is limited and mixed, so if it were the reality of God, He would not encompass all things. Each essence is incompatible with another; without existence, essences would not share their natures. Real existence, by contrast, is unity and breadth, and does not conflict with essences. Every essence is an existent in the ordinary predicative sense. One more argument: every real thing is either existence or essence. All essences are alike in being neither existence nor nonexistence, and essence is therefore not fit for the divine presence: in itself, it accepts either existence or nonexistence. Existence alone cannot accept nonexistence. — س قده

This point does not concern the theologians' argument. Even if existence were an added feature, they say that existence is caused, not essence. The author says that existence is fundamental and essence secondary, which might suggest that God's essence is caused by His existence even though that essence is necessary. He answers that essence is not made real apart from that existence. But essence, as you know, is a reflection of limited existence. Strictly speaking, God's pure existence has no essence in the disputed technical sense. What the author calls the secondary, uncreated essence consists of concepts that express the divine names and attributes, which point to unlimited existence. This is not the “essence” at issue in the debate, the natural universal. — س قده

This claim is surprising: a possible thing's existence is an accidental feature of its essence and is caused. It is an accident of essence, not an accident of existence, as explained more than once in the First Journey.
“The” refers back to the earlier argument. There, the cause was sought for existence itself; here, it is sought for being qualified by existence. — س قده

This assumes the primacy of existence. On that view, God's essence cannot be a necessary essence that is caused to be qualified by existence; it cannot belong to the level of the divine essence. It would instead be one of the derivative features, like relational attributes or concepts of the beautiful names, as we have said. Also, existence is not something added to essence; it is what makes essence real. So saying that essence is qualified by existence because of existence is like saying “a real essence exists,” even though essence in itself is equally open to existing or not existing.

Perhaps the speaker means to raise a third or even a fourth possibility, as in the later words, “and also for the investigator…” In that case, the alternatives would not form a strict division. If someone says that the supposed essence of God is simply a nature that does not resist nonexistence, or that unlimited luminous existence gives rise to an essence, we can allow those claims. But they would be separate arguments, not this one, even if they agree with its lofty conclusion. — س قده

You might object that this premise is not part of the argument. Someone who thinks existence is additional to God's essence may accept that God's existence depends on His own essence, while denying that it depends on anything else. Notice, however, that the argument's problem is not dependence but that something would have to precede itself. We answer that the author is addressing the circularity that seems to arise: the subject, essence, depends on its attribute, existence, while existence, insofar as it is an attribute, depends on its subject. — س قده

This assumes that existence is fundamental. If essence were fundamental, one could say that a necessary essence entails existence, so existence belongs to it necessarily, as evenness belongs to the number four. The claim that the Necessary Being is “what requires existence by its own nature” would then also be taken at face value. But both views are mistaken, because what necessarily entails existence must itself be existence or be surrounded by it.

Notice that the claim that God's essence is necessarily qualified by existence because existence follows from it is comparable to saying that an animal is necessarily qualified as human because humanity follows from it. Perhaps the comparison is intended only in this respect: the qualification is analytical, and the necessity comes from the defining feature, which is like existence. — س قده

They failed to notice that necessity is being considered in relation to real existence, and that real existence is what makes essence qualified by existence. They also missed a basic point in the argument: even if God had an essence, and that essence were only a mental consideration, existence would not become an external accident. If it did, essence would become the subject that bears it, and would itself be only an analytical feature.

The author interprets Dawānī this way even though Dawānī explicitly calls God an existence that subsists through itself, because Dawānī strongly favors the primacy of essence and treats existence as only a mental consideration. A thing must be either essence or existence. If existence is only conceptual, then of these two, God belongs to the side of essence. In Dawānī's account, existence is only the source from which the concept of existence is drawn. To speak of God as an individual instance of existence would therefore depart from his view.

If Dawānī wanted to avoid that departure, he could have used the wording of the careful investigator: God is pure existence, as philosophers say He is pure existent. This means that other things are like the letters alif and bāʾ—each is something existent—while He is simply existent, with nothing more to say of Him. His essence deserves to be called existent in itself, without qualification or cause. A possible essence, by contrast, deserves in itself to be called neither existent nor nonexistent. This account, too, is far from the truth.

You might say that Dawānī treats existence as conceptual because a possible thing has no individual existence of its own; for him, a possible thing exists by being related to God's self-subsisting existence. We answer: if a concept has something corresponding to it outside the mind, even if there is only one such instance, then it is real, not merely conceptual. The sun is not merely conceptual just because there is only one sun.

This applies if “possible” means its existence. If it means its essence, then it refers to another aspect that does not resist either existence or nonexistence. But because essence is only a mental consideration, this aspect is an accident. — س قده

This objection is not accepted. First, if the Necessary Being had an essence, it would have a unique level that belongs to no other thing: the level of its essence, which is distinct from all other essences in itself. That essence would determine its level of existence, the highest level in the graded reality of existence. Its existence in other levels would mean only that every effect depends on it as the First Cause, not that it is necessarily present in those levels.

Second, the critic may say that this feature belongs only to possible essences, not to essence as such—including an essence supposed to belong to the Necessary Being. Third, the claim that things have known forms in the higher principles is acceptable only of direct knowledge; what is known in that way is their existences, not their essences. As for knowledge through mental forms, whose objects are universal essences, the author's earlier account of how universals exist in the mind rules out such knowledge in beings that are immaterial in both essence and action.

There is another way to show that God has no essence. If He necessarily exists in Himself, then His existence must hold under every supposition. Whatever existent we suppose, in whatever way we suppose it, He exists with it. Even if we suppose nothing, that too is a supposition, and He still exists. So His existence is unrestricted, not limited by any condition. If it depended on a condition, it would be absent when that condition was removed, contrary to the premise that it exists under every supposition. It is therefore absolute and unlimited. He has no essence: if He had one, it would be distinct from other essences, and would necessarily be absent whenever they were present, contradicting the claim that He exists under every supposition. So the Necessary Being has no essence. — May his shadow endure.
That is, even if the thing is present through another existence in an incidental way, as it is in our minds and in higher minds. Essences have earlier and later stages of presence. — س قده
Yet He has a level that they do not share. As the saying goes: “Praise be to God, whose proof is that no state is without His presence.”
If the Necessary Being is simple in every respect, the concept “necessary being” is predicated of the whole reality. If it were predicated of only part of Him, He would be composite.

If necessary existence is not something added to God, then there is no essence in Him that could make Him many. A thing does not become two merely by itself. How, then, could His particular existence—identical with His individuality—become many? — س قده

The questioner accepts that God’s particular existence is identical with His individual identity, but denies that this prevents another such identity. If each were simple in itself, why could two wholly different simple identities not exist? — س قده

Ibn Kamuna’s objection bears most strongly on two groups. The first holds that essences are fundamental and intrinsically diverse, while existence is only an abstract concept. If God’s reality is an essence in the same way possible things are, these thinkers can allow two simple essences to differ completely, just as the most general kinds do. They can also distinguish a general title from what it describes, and so avoid the claims that the two realities must be composite or depend on something else for their individuality. The objection also challenges those who deny any likeness between cause and effect—or between one existence and another—even if they say existence has one shared meaning. If causes and effects need have no likeness, why could two necessary causes not differ completely? The objection is easy to answer on the view defended here: existence is real, simple, luminous, and graded. Its common meaning relates to its reality as a universal idea relates to a real individual, not as an abstract concept relates to what it describes.

Our teacher says that Ibn Kamuna’s objection does not trouble most philosophers who treat essence as fundamental, since they still hold that God is pure, simple existence, with no essence to which existence is added. They have also proved God’s oneness on this basis. The objection does trouble those who treat existence as merely mental even in God, making existence a feature that follows from an unknowable essence. They cannot answer as above; they must say that one concept cannot be drawn from two realities that have nothing in common. But that would require a shared feature in those realities, and so composition in God.

Some mystics call God the source from which “existent” is drawn; the Illuminationists call Him the Light of Lights, and the Aristotle’s followers call Him real existence. The intended answer is that one concept cannot be drawn from realities that are wholly different in themselves. In the true account, the shared idea of existence is drawn from the unity that possible essences have through their relation to God: God’s existence is what makes the concept apply both to Him and to things. The same would have to be true of two supposed Necessary Beings. But this answer does not fit a view that denies the reality of existence. If “relation” means the real giving of existence, it names the very doctrine that view rejects. If it means only a relation between concepts, then it follows the multiplicity of the essences and cannot unite them. — س قده
“What makes a thing what it is”: for both supposed beings, this would be necessary existence itself. — س قده
Rather, the difference would come from something else. If one shared meaning became many through matter or other features, the Necessary Being would depend on something else to be an individual.
If the supposed beings had the same essence, they would differ in individuality; if they had different essences, they would differ in necessary existence, which is one shared meaning. — س قده

This seems to refer to the proof that God has no essence. If the nature of an essence, a part of it, or something inseparable from it required multiplicity, there could be no single instance of that essence; every instance would have to be many. But if multiplicity came from something outside the essence, the instances would be caused by that external thing. So a Necessary Being divided into numerically many beings would be caused.
This relies on a view attributed to the author: calling knowledge a “quality” is only a loose way of speaking. In reality, knowledge of each category belongs to that category. — ط مد ظله

Rationality is not a bodily quality or passive state that could define a substance. Strictly speaking, reason is the power to grasp universals; that grasp is a relational quality, and the soul’s receiving it is a kind of change. Sense perception, which grasps particulars, is likewise a quality and change. Motion, too, is an unstable accident and cannot define a substance. The author does not enter into these technical points because he is discussing the ordinary meanings of words. In ordinary speech, “rational” means a being that has outward speech or reason; “having” expresses a relation. — س قده

You might say this case differs from the first only in being broader or narrower. The reply is that this second kind of usage is unrestricted: the relation need not follow ordinary language or convention, since the truth of things is not bound by either. The author points out that ordinary speech often uses derived words to mean “related to,” as in words for a milk seller, date seller, or grocer. The Qur'anic phrase “I am not unjust to the servants” can also mean “I am not one who does injustice.” A derived word can even name the source itself. This supports the claim that a source need not be present in its subject in just one fixed way.
This refers to the broader meaning just described, so it does not repeat the question’s earlier point that “existent” is a general concept. — س قده
This is the distributive universal, not the universal considered as applying to everything at once. The thing that produces effects, or that in which existence is present, is the logical universal.

In essences related to existence, real existence does not inhere in them, but the shared concept “existence” does apply to them as a derived idea. This wider concept also applies to existence that subsists through itself.

If the concept of existence is considered as a title that carries its judgment into the reality it describes, then it has no separate recipient or source of action. If it is considered as a mental object in its own right, it has a mental source, the mind. Looking closely at the shared concept also shows that its instances and the realities from which it is drawn must be one: if two things had wholly different features, neither could qualify as an instance of the same concept without some common ground. — س قده

The objection concerns real existence being added to an essence in the outside world. A mental concept may still be analytically attributed to another concept, as one abstract idea applies to the thing from which it is abstracted. When philosophers say that existence is added to essence, they mean this kind of addition in thought.

Arabic sometimes forms words by analogy, as when one says “the clay turned to stone” or “the camel turned into a she-camel.” But this is an exception to the usual rule and should not be extended without clear evidence—especially to the common word “existent,” used of both God and possible things. More broadly, the author is discussing how words are formed from verbal sources. Such a source is normally an abstract meaning that can take different forms, unlike a fixed noun such as “iron.” — س قده

Earlier grammarians treated the verbal noun as the source from which derived words are formed. Later scholars instead located the source in the root letters shared by those words, while each word’s form expresses a different relation to that source. A derived adjective can express a relation to its source in several ways: directly, as striking relates to the one who strikes, or by an accepted kind of usage, as “iron worker” relates to iron or “sun-warmed” relates to the sun. If there is figurative extension, it lies in the meaning of the source, not in the grammatical form of the derived word. The critic’s examples therefore do not show that a rigid noun such as “iron” itself can be the source of a derived word; nor do they prove that the source must be literally present in its subject. — ط مد ظله

The word “existent” can be applied to existence itself, just as “white” can be applied to whiteness and “hot” to heat. The standard for a derived word is that its source be either present in the subject or real in it in some other way; one specific relation need not always apply. — س قده

One version of the text adds “and,” but that reading is not sound. The examples are meant to explain figurative extension. The “source” is whatever makes the derived word applicable, not necessarily the technical source from which a word is grammatically formed. — س قده

The blacksmith is related to iron so closely that it dominates his thought and work; this can be described figuratively as his having a share in iron. It does not mean that merely imagining iron makes someone a blacksmith. — س قده
The image of the sun is present in the warmed water; “sun” can also be used for the sun’s rays. — س قده

If everyday word use is too ambiguous to establish philosophical truths, it is especially unreliable in cases that could mean relation, figurative realization, or literal presence. The author first says not to infer truth from common expressions, then notes that even ordinary usage does not always require a source to be present in its subject. If we examine usage carefully, he argues, it supports the conclusion required by reason. — س قده

Dawānī's point, as I understand it, is not that the reality of existence is itself a word or an idea. The source from which a word is formed belongs to language: one word may be formed from another. The reality of existence is neither a word nor a concept. How could it literally be the linguistic source from which the word “existent,” or its general meaning, is derived?

It is a source in a different sense: the real existence from which the mind draws the concepts “existence” and “existent,” and to which those concepts point. We speak in a similar way when we call a real defining feature the source of the feature expressed in a logical definition.

Dawānī also says that the source of the word “existent” can be something that exists through itself. This makes sense if he is speaking of the real thing named by the expression. It can also make sense if he treats the expression as a way of attending to the real thing, so that a judgment about the expression points through it to reality. That is how a term works in a statement about a whole class, rather than a statement about a nature considered only as a nature.

The concept and the reality it describes are different, but not so unrelated that we cannot pass from the first to the second. A thing's appearance is that thing understood through one of its faces; otherwise a judgment about the appearance could tell us nothing about the thing.

Existence, then, has both a concept and a reality. The concept is a name and a way of looking; the reality is what the name reveals. Some statements, such as statements about how words are formed, belong to the concept. Other statements, such as “it exists through itself,” belong to the reality. This is why the author says in The Beginning and the Return that the fact that a derived expression is a matter of thought does not make the reality from which it is drawn unreal. — س قده

Dawānī may mean that real existence, considered as the source of the word “existent,” becomes a general concept. But God’s being a true individual instance of “existent” does not make Him a universal or a particular in the ordinary logical sense. — ط مد ظله

The reply is that knowledge of God is innate: God is so clear and radiant that His very fullness of light hides Him from us. Everyone knows himself through direct awareness, though this awareness has degrees, and direct awareness of oneself cannot be separated from awareness of one’s source. This kind of inborn knowledge is enough to explain our use of words for God. If God is also the one who gave words their meanings, there is no difficulty.
One possible answer is to interpret “source” broadly enough to include both God and possible things. — ط مد ظله

The critic says that sometimes “existent” is derived from “existence,” and sometimes from the relation to existence. The reply is that a derived word and its source must correspond in both sound and meaning. If “existent” means existence itself, it is derived from existence; if it means something related to existence, it is derived from that relation. The author may also use “source” to mean what makes the word applicable, not only a verbal noun. — س قده

“Blacksmith” consistently means someone related to iron, never iron itself, so it is not a close parallel to “existent.” Dawānī tries to give “existent” one broad meaning: either what produces effects or what has existence. But the first meaning has no trace of existence in it, while the second does not fit “existent” when it means merely “related to existence.” Real existence can be a subject in its own right, but then “existent” is no longer a general term shared by God and other things. The author’s point is not merely that common usage determines the meaning; it is that reason supports the ordinary meaning, unless proof shows otherwise. — س قده

This is a strong objection. If God is real existence, then existence is real; the fact that it has no many instances inhering in essences does not make it a mere mental idea. A nature is real if even one real instance exists. Some later philosophers try to say that possible existences are not themselves instances of existence, since the outside world contains only essences, and that God is an incidental instance. But this does not resolve the problem on the author’s terms.

Dawānī’s discussion seems inconsistent: he says that if existence is considered on its own it has no existence in something else, but elsewhere says it cannot exist apart from another. The issue is more than whether existence is fundamental; it is whether it is real at all. — س قده
As noted earlier, the argument confuses a concept with its individual reality. Calling God “particular existence” is only a technical expression for those who treat existence as conceptual.

The alternatives may concern whether the critic consciously distinguishes a thing’s being qualified by something from that quality’s inhering in it, or confuses the two. The author uses both expressions at times without distinction. More precisely, a quality’s inherence is the feature that makes predication possible; being qualified is the relation expressed by the judgment. A second-order concept may exist only in the mind while applying to something in reality, as with possibility or “thingness.” — س قده

A subtle case does not require a more obvious case in which the essence and its attribute have separate existences. To say that a quality is added to essence requires only that the essence exist; it does not require an existence separate from that quality. A quality added to existence, by contrast, requires an independently existing subject.

The author is distinguishing the mystics’ “unity of existence” from the view that existence and existent are one reality whose levels are many. On the first view, essences are real and many, while existence is a mental concept; beings are united only by being related to existence. The author argues that this does not yield the deeper unity of existence. On his own view, existence is a real, graded light: each particular existence is a level of it, and relations between levels express the one reality. The parts of the world are therefore united more deeply than by contact or dependence. At the highest level of the created world, the complete human being gathers the forms of all other kinds of being, as a final form gathers the earlier forms within it. All things depend on that final form for their full actuality, and it in turn depends on God, the One who sustains all. The changing stages of the world are gathered in an enduring reality, just as the same human being remains while bodily conditions change.

Those who say that a collection exists as one thing usually mean that all its members together exist, not that the arrangement of the members forms a separate reality. Some later scholars, including al-Lahiji, do treat the whole as a distinct existent; some proofs of God’s existence rely on that assumption. — س قده
Otherwise, one possibility would be preferred over another without any reason. — س قده
A cause must precede its effect. This applies to the whole understood as a single reality, not to all the members simply taken together. See al-Lahiji’s Shawāriq. — س قده
In this example the Necessary Being alone is the complete cause of the first effect. Once that effect exists, the pair is a whole; no further cause is needed to make the whole.

If the argument is only a trick, the author’s criticism stands. If it comes from a philosopher who sees God as necessary in every respect, it may mean that God is present at every level of existence and with every existent, yet has no separate essence at any one level.
The argument would be sound if it said that both unity and multiplicity are caused, rather than saying multiplicity is possible in relation to necessary existence. — س قده

Dawānī treats existence as a mental concept and holds that everything outside the mind is an essence. So he interprets “God is pure existence” to mean “God is pure existent”: since existence has no real instance, God cannot be existence. This is only a verbal dispute. In reality, a thing is either real existence or an essence; there is no third kind.

This approach reverses the true one. On the true view, an essence is existent by being one with a real level of existence, from which the concept of existence is drawn. The essence itself has no separate counterpart in reality; it is indeterminate and disappears into the existence that makes it real. Dawānī instead denies any real instance of existence and says that an essence becomes existent by being one with the concept “existent.” The two views are opposite, though Dawānī’s rejection of a real split between essence and existence may seem close to the truth. His view still leaves possible essences as the real things, and it cannot explain why they deserve to be called existent.

On Dawānī’s account, the concept of existence is shared and mental, while its application to real existence is either figurative or based on another use of the word. This would make God have existence twice: as His own reality and as an instance of the shared concept. But the same problem applies to Dawānī’s account, since he treats God’s real existence as an instance of the general concept.

The author is presenting the consequence of Dawānī’s view, not endorsing it. If God’s essence is not a real instance of existence, then saying He is an existent means only that an abstract concept applies to Him. But Dawānī also says that existence does not inhere in an essence. His own account therefore faces the same difficulty. — س قده

A particular human being is a nature of humanity surrounded by individuating features. The universal nature and its particular instance are not two separate existences. Likewise, “existent” applies to particular existence as an external predicate, not as a quality added to it. — س قده

The discussion of mental analysis here does not yet answer Dawānī’s second objection. It only shows that a particular existence and the general concept do not amount to two separate existences in God, as a possible thing can be analyzed into what does not resist existence and what does.

An essence, in the technical sense, is a bounded nature that can be thought of as universal or particular and that does not in itself require existence or nonexistence. Any limited nature is an essence. Existence, knowledge, power, life, and the divine names point instead to unlimited reality, so God has no essence in that technical sense. “Essence” can also mean more generally what makes a thing what it is or answers the question “What is it?” — س قده

The concept of existence relates to its real instance as an essential feature relates to the thing it describes: it reflects that reality, unlike a merely added quality. But the real nature of existence cannot be present in the mind without being changed into a concept. So the shared concept does not literally become part of the individual reality it describes. This is why Sadra can call existence a second-order concept while holding that existence itself is real.
These are the possible essences, which are dependent features of actual existence. — س قده

One might ask how Dawānī can say that “existent” is identical with a possible essence when he denies that a real or mental instance of existence is present in the essence. The strongest version of his view is that both God and possible things are sources from which the concept “existent” is drawn: God is that source through Himself, while a possible essence is such a source only because it has been brought into relation with its maker. But this relation is itself existence. What makes God and possible things existent is therefore the reality of existence, even if one avoids that name.

“Confusing kinds of predication” here is not the familiar fallacy of attaching an unrelated condition to a subject. The mistake is to confuse strict, meaning-based predication with ordinary predication. A concept is always itself in meaning, but it is not always an actual instance of itself. — س قده

The true subject of metaphysics is unrestricted real existence: existence in its full reach, not limited to any one nature. When philosophers call “unrestricted existent” the subject of the science, they mean the real nature as it appears in its instances, not the universal concept alone. The fallacy comes from leaving out that qualification. — مره

The argument also risks confusing what is actually present to the mind with what the mind could analyze if it were present. A thing may be analyzable in principle even if it cannot exist as a mental image. This is another case of treating an abstract description as though it were the reality itself.
The concept of existence is self-evident; its real nature is the light and manifestation itself.

The author uses blackness as an example of a simple reality that can be present in itself or in another thing. Blackness also evokes darkness, which helps suggest how all distinctions and traces of other things disappear within the simple, luminous reality of existence.

There are three levels of oneness: the oneness of necessary existence, already proved; the special oneness of real existence, which will be discussed later; and the oneness of God as the sole deity and creator, established here. The first does not by itself prove the third. For example, the Muʿtazilites held that human beings act independently through their own power; another view would say that God created the first intellect and then left it to act on its own. That is not the philosophers’ position. For them, God alone gives existence; separate intellects, souls, and natural causes are only means through which His generosity and giving reach things. Only what is free of potentiality can give existence. — س قده

In short, nothing comes to exist by itself. All things receive existence from God, both when they first come to be and for as long as they continue to exist. The act of bringing something into being follows from the reality of existence itself. — س قده

The sun analogy is only a starting point; God’s relation to things is not literally like sunlight. Sunlight spreads over surfaces and visible things, while the light of existence reaches everything sensed, imagined, conceived, and beyond. Sunlight touches only the outer surfaces; existence reaches into the depths of things and makes them depend on itself. Sunlight is not aware, while the levels of the light of existence are living and aware. Sunlight also fades and has other lights beside it; the light of the Real never fades and has no second.

Grammatically, “alike in nature” describes the elements; “in different places” describes how they are situated. — س قده

They would be separated in the sense of occupying different places, but could not remain permanently apart after first being naturally joined. Otherwise there would be empty space in the worlds from which they came and into which they moved, ruptures and joins in the spheres, and heavy bodies moving outward. All these results are impossible.

“First” refers to the beginning of the separation, and “return” to its end. The argument concerns all worlds, not only their elements. A permanent division of two bodies of the same kind—for example, two suns or two spheres—would require permanent force, but the heavens are not moved by force. They would have to return to natural unity, which would also bring the earlier contradictions. Ordinary individuals of one kind in our world are different: each individual passes away, while the kind continues only through successive individuals. The argument also rules out a world naturally made of many separate individuals from the start: their like parts would have to be separate too, yielding multiplicity without any unity.

Natural place is essential to a body of a given nature and cannot vary. If the places themselves joined together, place would have to move and have another place of its own. Nor can what is the center become an outer edge. — س قده
Such a union is possible in itself, even if the physical arrangement of the world would prevent it from actually occurring because it would require empty space or a break in the heavens. — س قده

Avicenna argues that no different natural movement or sensible quality means there can be no naturally different bodily world. One might object that the same effect can arise from different causes—for example, heat from fire, anger, movement, or the sun. The reply is that this resemblance holds only at a broad level; on closer examination, the kinds of heat differ. Even “evenness,” which applies to four, eight, and other numbers, is an abstract feature with no separate instance in them. Abstract features follow the things from which they are drawn, and one concept cannot come from wholly different things precisely as different. — س قده
The author first divides straight movement into three kinds, then revises this to a two-way division: movement either toward or away from the center.

The nineteen qualities are nine familiar simple tastes, four active and passive tangible qualities, three qualities of hearing, sight, and smell, and three qualities sensed indirectly. It would be more precise to list the basic tangible qualities individually. The author’s point is that the natural world has an ordered governance; as the active intellect governs this world in the philosophers’ account, so a governing power oversees the elemental world. — س قده
